# Proof

**Claim:** There exists a continuous injective map from $\mathbb{Q}$ to $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$.

## Construction

Define
$$
f:\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q},\qquad f(q)=q+\sqrt{2}.
$$

## Verification

**The image lies in $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$.**  
Let $q\in\mathbb{Q}$. If $q+\sqrt{2}$ were rational, then $\sqrt{2}=(q+\sqrt{2})-q$ would be rational (a difference of two rationals), contradicting the irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$. Hence $f(q)\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$.

**Injectivity.**  
If $f(q_1)=f(q_2)$, then $q_1+\sqrt{2}=q_2+\sqrt{2}$, so $q_1=q_2$. Thus $f$ is injective.

**Continuity.**  
The map $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $g(x)=x+\sqrt{2}$ is continuous (it is a translation). Its restriction to $\mathbb{Q}$ is therefore continuous as a map $\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{R}$ (where $\mathbb{Q}$ carries the subspace topology from $\mathbb{R}$). Since the image of this restriction is contained in $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ carries the subspace topology from $\mathbb{R}$, the universal property of the subspace topology guarantees that the corestriction
$$
f:\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}
$$
is continuous. (Explicitly: for any open set $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, we have $U=V\cap(\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q})$ for some open $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, and $f^{-1}(U)=g|_{\mathbb{Q}}^{-1}(V)$, which is open in $\mathbb{Q}$ since $g|_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is continuous.)

## Conclusion

The map $f(q)=q+\sqrt{2}$ is a continuous injective map from $\mathbb{Q}$ to $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$. Therefore, **such a map exists**.

### PROOF COMPLETE
